Returns a JSON string; parse it.Psalm 24: verse-by-verse research notes

I read nine pages in full or in large part: Enduring Word (Guzik), Gill, the Pulpit Commentary, Spurgeon's *Treasury of David*, Matthew Henry, the Bible Hub pages that collect several commentaries for vv. 1, 4, 7, 8 and 10, StudyLight's verse pages, Bible.org, GotQuestions and Augustine on NewAdvent. My search and fetch tools then hit their usage limit. Because of that I couldn't reach NET Bible notes, OCA, catholic.com, Wesley, the Lutheran sites, Desiring God or Ligonier. Nothing below comes from those sites.

**Overview / title**
- Many link the psalm to the Ark being brought into Jerusalem (2 Samuel 6). Guzik agrees with Spurgeon that David was also looking ahead to Christ's ascension. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Poole (on Bible Hub) says David also had in mind the temple Solomon would later build. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-1.htm
- Gill says David wrote it by the Spirit as a prophecy of Christ and the gospel church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- The Pulpit Commentary mentions Ewald's view that the psalm was first two separate pieces (vv. 1–6 and 7–10). It argues instead that it was one piece from the start, held together by God's glory and the climb up Zion. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html

**v. 1**
- David ruled a small kingdom, yet he knew Israel's covenant God owned the whole earth, everything in it and every person on it. Guzik notes that Satan is called "god of this age" but acts only as God allows. Paul quotes this verse in 1 Corinthians 10:26, 28 to show that no food really belongs to idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Spurgeon contrasts the verse with the later Jewish idea that only the holy land and Abraham's children belonged to God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-1.htm
- Barnes says all human ownership comes second to God's claim. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-1.htm
- Gill also applies the verse to Christ as Lord of all, linking it to the Shepherd of Psalm 23. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- Matthew Henry draws two lessons: be content with what God has given you, and don't envy others. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_024.cfm
- The Pulpit Commentary says no lesser "demiurge" made or rules the world; God alone does. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/24-1.html

**v. 2**
- God's ownership rests on his having made the world. Guzik connects the verse to dry land appearing out of the waters on the third day (Genesis 1). He quotes Kidner that "upon" could mean "above." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Gill gives other renderings ("with" or "by" the seas). He also mentions a theory that before the Flood the earth was a crust over the waters. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- Henry says that a world founded on water reminds us how unstable earthly things are. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_024.cfm

**v. 3**
- Guzik: the question is about who has the right to stand before God, and it is the most important question there is. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: God's real "hill" is the highest heaven. It suggests David meant the question as a warning to the Levites to make themselves pure before carrying the Ark. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html
- Gill reads the hill as Zion or Moriah, but in a deeper sense as the church. He compares the 144,000 on Mount Zion in Revelation 14:1. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/24-3.html

**v. 4**
- Guzik: "hands" means actions and "heart" means motives. He quotes Kidner that "lift up the soul" means to trust (compare Psalm 25:1). He says only Jesus fully meets this standard, and believers stand in his righteousness. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Gill: the pure heart comes first, and clean hands flow from it. No one has a pure heart by nature; God makes the heart clean by faith and Christ's blood. Clean hands mean a generally upright life, not a sinless one, and they don't justify anyone. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- Ellicott: the Hebrew margin reads "*my* soul." The rabbis took this to mean taking God's *name* in vain, and "vanity" here means falsehood. https://biblehub.com/psalms/24-4.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: a worshipper must be right in deed, thought and word. It calls false swearing one of the worst sins of the tongue. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html
- Henry: not lifting up the soul to vanity means not setting your heart on wealth, praise or pleasure. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_024.cfm

**v. 5**
- Guzik: the "righteousness" here is *received* from God. He says salvation was never by works, even under the Old Covenant; blessing might follow obedience, but righteousness always came from God. He quotes Clarke, who thinks the verse may allude to Obed-edom's blessing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Gill: this means righteousness from Christ, received by faith, together with forgiveness and adoption. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- Pulpit Commentary: God gives the honest-hearted further graces, such as justification, assurance and perseverance. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html
- Henry: "we have no righteousness of our own." https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_024.cfm

**v. 6**
- Guzik: "Jacob" stands for God's covenant people, and every generation has to seek God anew. The repetition and the *Selah* add emphasis. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: the Greek Old Testament (LXX) reads "God of Jacob," and the Hebrew may have lost a word. It prefers to keep the Hebrew and read "even Jacob," meaning the true Israel (Romans 9:6). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html
- Gill: "face" means God's favour. He also mentions readings that apply "Jacob" to God, to Christ, or to the church. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm

**v. 7**
- Ellicott: "ancient doors" fits the old gates of the Jebusite fortress. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-7.htm
- Maclaren pictures two half-choirs, one inside the gates and one outside. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-7.htm
- Poole and Benson list the possible gates: Zion's city gates, the tabernacle, or the temple seen ahead by prophecy. They also apply it to Christ entering his church, believers' hearts, or heaven at his ascension. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-7.htm
- Guzik sees three fulfilments: the Ark coming to Jerusalem, Christ entering heaven, and Jesus entering a heart that opens to him (Revelation 3:20). He cites Boice, who says the psalm was used in temple worship on the first day of the week. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Henry: heaven's gates were shut against us since Genesis 3:24. Christ, having made atonement, demands they open, for us as well as for himself. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_024.cfm
- GotQuestions: the gates are addressed as if they were people. It links the "glory" to the cloud of glory over the Ark. https://www.gotquestions.org/King-of-glory.html

**v. 8**
- Guzik quotes Kidner that "mighty in battle" echoes the "warrior" of Exodus 15:3. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Pulpit Commentary: the other half of the choir, acting as door-keepers, asks the question as if they didn't know the answer. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-8.htm
- Barnes: the title may recall victories won with the Ark present among Israel's armies. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-8.htm
- Spurgeon: the watchers on the walls ask who this is, and the answer comes back in a great wave of music. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps024.cfm
- GotQuestions: the Hebrew word for "glory," *kabod*, means "weight," so the King of glory is the one to be taken most seriously. https://www.gotquestions.org/King-of-glory.html

**v. 9**
- The repetition adds emphasis (Guzik). The Pulpit Commentary says the first choir repeats its challenge. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/ ; https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/24-9.html
- Gill: the call is repeated because churches and believers are slow to open to Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/24-9.html

**v. 10**
- The Cambridge Bible says this is the high point. "LORD of hosts" makes its first appearance in the Psalms here, presenting God as ruler of heaven's powers and of the whole universe. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-10.htm
- Maclaren (quoted by Guzik) describes the universe as God's disciplined army. Guzik links the verse to the crowd's question at the Triumphal Entry, "Who is this?" (Matthew 21:10). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
- Spurgeon: the ascended Saviour is declared Head of the universe. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/spurgeon_charles/tod/ps024.cfm
- Henry also applies the verse to Christ's second coming. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/24-10.htm

**Where Protestant readers differ (only what I found)**
- **vv. 4–5, how the standard relates to grace.** These are differences of emphasis, not traditions I could confirm from each tradition's own sites:
  - Gill (Baptist, Calvinist) says purity of heart is God's work, and clean hands never justify. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
  - Guzik (Calvary Chapel) says a holy life was the *condition* of fellowship under the Old Covenant and is the *result* of it under the New. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-24/
  - The Pulpit Commentary presents justification as a grace given to the honest-hearted worshipper. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-24.html
- **vv. 7–10, the "open your heart" reading.** Guzik, Trapp, Henry and Gill apply the gates to individual hearts or the church, alongside the ascension reading. I found no Protestant source that rejects this.

**Other views**
- **Augustine (Catholic, Church Father):** the "gates" are worldly rulers and the hold of desire and fear, and the everlasting doors are the way into eternal life. "Mighty in battle" means Christ's victory over death; the risen Lord's wounds are healed. In v. 10 the "prince of the power of the air" is pictured asking in amazement who this King is. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801024.htm
- **Descent into hell (harrowing of hell):** Gill describes a Catholic reading of vv. 7–10 in which the gates are hell's gates and Christ goes down to free the Old Testament saints held in "limbus patrum." He rejects it on the grounds that those saints were already in bliss. This is a Protestant's account of the view; I couldn't reach a Catholic or Orthodox source to see how they state it themselves. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- **Jewish reading:** Gill reports that Jewish interpreters, including the Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase), took the gates to be the temple gates at Solomon's dedication. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/psalms/24.htm
- **Modern scholarship, Orthodox use, and prosperity or word-of-faith teaching:** none of the pages I read covered these, so I've left them out.
